Header: Phthorimaea operculella Amharic: dinche borebori esaterate; Tigrigna: hamokshtay

Prevention: Use clean and healthy tuber seeds for planting.
These are available from farmers corporatives

Deep ploughing during field preparation, in addition to deep planting of tuber seed at a depth of 5-10cm prevents female moths from laying eggs on the tubers and reduces larvae migration to tubers in the soil
Earthening (hilling) up two weeks after planting protects from female moths laying their eggs and reduces migration of larvae to reach the tubers
Frequent and adequate irrigation prevents the formation of cracks in the soil that female moths use to reach the tubers to lay their eggs
When the crop is mature, harvest healthy tubers in one go and remove harvest residues and burn
Crop rotation with cereals and pulse crops is useful to decrease pest build up
Monitoring: The larvae can attack the leaves, stems and tubers of potato plants.
These are 12mm long with a greyish/green body and a dark brown head
Larvae may be seen tunneling through leaf and stem tissue
Early symptoms may not be visible in tubers externally.
Cut tubers open, look inside for larvae, damage (tunnels) and frass (waste).
Check tubers in storage every 2 weeks.
Also look for circular holes (2-3mm) on the surface of the tuber
If the tubers have been infected for a long time, the tuber may be rotten
Adult moths are most active at night.
They are small (1cm long) with a winfspan of 15-17mm
Take action when symptoms of the pest are detected
Direct Control: Carefully remove damaged or infested tubers and bury to reduce severity of the infestation
Use diffused lighting in stores for tubers to be used for seed purposes.
This makes tubers appear green hence unsuitable for moths to lay eggs on.
Cover the stored harvested tubers immediately to prevent female moths, reaching the tuber and laying their eggs
Restrictions: There are no registered insecticides in
Ethiopia for the management of potato tuber moth
